days.title: Scaling Projects, Plan Modes and Applying Safely

concepts.heading: Why and How to Split a Large Project
concepts.body: A configuration and its state are one unit: every plan refreshes every object in the state, and every apply can touch any of them. A root module with networking, a database tier and dozens of services therefore has slow plans and a large blast radius, because a typo in a service change can sit in the same plan as the database. Raising `-parallelism` does not help much, since the docs say Terraform does not use it to handle API rate limits. The recommended fix is several smaller configurations, each with its own state, split along ownership (network team, platform team, app team) and change frequency (foundation rarely, services daily). A separate state also means a separate lock, access policy and apply history. The price is coupling work: producers must be applied before consumers, and values move through outputs or data sources. Routine `-target` is not the answer; the docs reserve it for exceptional cases, and it leaves the state out of step with the configuration. Splitting is a governance and runtime decision, not a file-layout one: repeated module calls with different names or `for_each` keys coexist happily in one state.

concepts.heading: Sharing Values Between States
concepts.body: After a split, configuration B often needs an object from configuration A. `terraform_remote_state` reads the latest state snapshot from A's backend and returns only A's root module outputs. Three practical rules follow. First, only root outputs are visible: an output of `module.vpc` reaches consumers only if the root re-exports it with its own `output` block, and the producer must be applied after that output is added or the consumer fails with output not found. Second, the reader needs access to the whole state snapshot, which often holds secrets, so a security reviewer is right to object. Third, with the S3 backend the data source's `workspace` argument defaults to the producer's default workspace, so a `prod` consumer silently receives dev data unless it sets `workspace = terraform.workspace` or points at a different key. Narrower alternatives are a key/value store or DNS record published by A and read with a matching data source, or tags looked up with a provider data source. The `defaults` argument supplies fallback outputs when the state is empty, which helps bootstrap but can mask a missing apply.

concepts.heading: Plan Modes and Options
concepts.body: Plan has three modes: normal (reconcile with the configuration), `-destroy` (plan removal of every managed object) and `-refresh-only` (plan to update state and root outputs with real values, changing no resource). Options adjust a mode. `-replace=ADDRESS` plans a replacement of one instance even when nothing differs, which is how you rebuild a corrupted but healthy-looking server; it succeeds `terraform taint` and cannot be combined with `-destroy`. `-refresh-only` is the answer when someone resized a database in the console and you want the state to record it: afterwards, the next normal plan will still propose reverting it unless the code is updated too. `-refresh=false` skips the read of real objects, which is faster and gentler on throttled APIs but means out-of-band changes are missing from the plan. `-target` narrows the scope and is for exceptional recovery only. `-detailed-exitcode` changes the status: 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes present, so a script treating every non-zero as failure will break on pending changes.

concepts.heading: Saved Plans and Their Rules
concepts.body: `terraform plan -out=tfplan` writes an opaque file with the full configuration, all planned values and all plan options, including input variables. Sensitive values are stored in cleartext even though the terminal hides them, so the artifact needs restricted access. Inspect it with `terraform show tfplan` or `-json`. Do not give it a `.tf` suffix, or Terraform tries to read it as configuration. Applying a saved plan is itself the approval: there is no prompt and `-auto-approve` is ignored. Because the file already holds the final decisions, Terraform rejects extra planning options such as `-var` on `terraform apply tfplan`; to change a value, plan again and review again. A saved plan records the state it was computed against. If another pipeline changed that state in between, apply fails with a stale plan error, and the fix is to re-plan, re-review and apply. A state lock is released between separate plan and apply jobs, so serialize runs per state in the CI system instead of relying on locking alone. The apply machine also needs the same providers (init with the same lock file) and Terraform version.

concepts.heading: Partial Failures and Tainted Objects
concepts.body: Terraform has no transactions and no rollback. State is written as the apply proceeds, so if 30 resources are planned and the 13th fails with an API error, the 12 that finished are recorded in state; independent operations already running normally complete, and dependents of the failed resource are not attempted. Read the error, fix the cause (permissions, quota, an invalid argument) and run plan again: it compares the configuration with the updated state and shows only the unfinished work, so rerunning is the recovery, not a manual cleanup. A resource whose creation failed after the remote object was partly built, for example because a provisioner failed, is saved as tainted. A tainted object is considered degraded, and the next plan proposes to replace it (destroy then create, or create then destroy with `create_before_destroy`). `terraform plan -replace=ADDRESS` gives the same result on demand, and `terraform untaint` marks an object healthy again once you have verified it. Never disable locking with `-lock=false` to get past errors during recovery.

examPoints: A question about a slow plan or a typo that reached the database is testing state boundaries: split by ownership and change frequency with separate states, not routine -target, higher -parallelism or CLI workspaces.
A question where a saved plan fails or is rejected is testing its rules: a stale plan after other state changes needs a new plan and review, and -var cannot be added to terraform apply tfplan.
A question about a pipeline that fails whenever changes exist is testing -detailed-exitcode, where exit code 2 means success with changes and 1 means error.

quiz.q: A console edit shrank a managed database. The team wants state to record the new size now, without touching infrastructure, and then decide about the code. Which command does that, and what will the next normal plan show if the code still has the old size?
choices: terraform plan -replace on the database; the next plan is empty because the new instance matches the code
terraform apply -refresh-only; the next plan proposes changing the database back to the size in the code
terraform plan -refresh=false; the next plan proposes nothing because the console size is accepted
terraform apply -target on the database; the next plan keeps the console size because -target updates the code
quiz.explain: Refresh-only updates state and outputs with real values and changes no resource, so the next normal plan compares the unchanged code with the new state and proposes to revert. Choice A rebuilds the database, C only skips reading real objects, and D narrows scope but never edits code.

quiz.q: A pipeline applies a reviewed file with `terraform apply -var="size=large" tfplan` and fails. A second pipeline had applied a change to the same state after the plan was made. What are the two problems?
choices: The file needs a .tf suffix, and -auto-approve is missing so the apply waits for a prompt
The plan is stale because the state changed, and a saved plan cannot take extra -var options
Locking was disabled for the plan, and the variable size is not declared in the saved file
The state moved to a new workspace, and the plan file must be regenerated with -destroy
quiz.explain: A saved plan fixes all planning options and variables, so -var is rejected, and Terraform refuses a plan computed against an older state. Choice A is wrong because a .tf suffix breaks the file and passing the plan counts as approval; C and D invent causes.

days.recap: Split by ownership and change rate into separate states; share root outputs only (workspace argument matters). Plan: -replace rebuilds, -refresh-only fixes state, -detailed-exitcode 2 means changes. Saved plans hold cleartext secrets, go stale, accept no extra options. Failed applies keep progress; re-plan, tainted means replace.

days.title: Import, Generated Configuration and Lifecycle Rules

concepts.heading: Declarative Import with import Blocks
concepts.body: An `import` block adopts an existing object into state as part of the normal workflow. It has `to` (the resource instance address) and `id` (the provider's ID string), plus optional `for_each` and `provider`. The `to` address must match a `resource` block unless configuration is generated. Because the block is evaluated during `terraform plan`, each import appears as `to import` in the plan, so fifty existing buckets can be reviewed in a pull request before anything is applied; `terraform apply` then records them. The older CLI command `terraform import ADDRESS ID` writes state immediately with no plan, no approval and no CI visibility, and also needs a resource block. Blocks may stay in version control as a record or be removed after the apply. The `id` must be known during planning: `id = aws_instance.base.id` for an instance created in the same apply is an error, because the import is planned before anything is created. Take the ID from variables, locals or data sources, or create the dependency in an earlier run. If `to` has no matching resource block and nothing generates one, plan fails and state is unchanged.

concepts.heading: Many Objects at Once and Reading the Next Plan
concepts.body: For resources created with `for_each`, one `import` block can adopt all of them. The block accepts `for_each` as a map or a set of strings, and `each.key` and `each.value` work inside `to` and `id`: `import { for_each = toset(var.names) to = aws_s3_bucket.b[each.key] id = each.value }`. The `to` must name the specific instance, here `aws_s3_bucket.b["logs"]`; `count` is not an argument of `import`. Import records state, it does not write your `.tf` files. After the apply, a plan that shows an in-place update to several arguments means the resource block disagrees with the real object, so the apply would change the object to match the code. Decide per argument whether to edit the code to reflect reality or accept the change, and iterate until the plan shows no changes. `terraform plan -generate-config-out=PATH` can draft resource blocks for import blocks that have none, writing a new file (an existing file is an error). The docs flag it as experimental, so treat its output as a draft to review and tidy, and do not build a process around it.

concepts.heading: Moving an Object Between States
concepts.body: A real object belongs to exactly one state entry. Moving a shared VPC out of a monolith into a new network configuration without destroying it means two steps in a fixed order: make the destination adopt the object, then make the source forget it. Adopt with an `import` block and a matching `resource` block in the new configuration. Forget in the old one with a `removed` block containing `lifecycle { destroy = false }`, or with `terraform state rm`. Simply deleting the resource block from the old configuration would plan a destroy, which is the trap. Import first, then remove, so the object always has an owner and the two states never both plan changes to it. The same idea answers a team that retires a resource from management but keeps it running. Afterwards the consumers of the old output must be repointed, which is another reason to apply producers before consumers. A saved plan or a lock held by another pipeline is not involved here; the mistake to avoid is two states claiming one object, because both would try to update or delete it.

concepts.heading: create_before_destroy and prevent_destroy
concepts.body: By default a forced replacement destroys the old object and then creates the new one. `create_before_destroy = true` reverses this for zero downtime, provided both objects can exist at once, so a fixed unique `name = "web-sg"` makes the replacement fail; use `name_prefix` or a generated suffix. Terraform propagates the ordering to dependencies: if A has it and depends on B, B implicitly gets it and the state records that, which is why you cannot set it to false on B (a cycle would result). It is the only lifecycle rule stored in state. A destroy-time provisioner does not run when `create_before_destroy` is set, so cleanup that relies on it silently never happens. `prevent_destroy = true` makes any plan that would destroy the object fail, including a replacement and `terraform destroy`. It is read from the configuration, so deleting the whole resource block deletes the rule too, and Terraform then plans a normal destroy. Use a `removed` block with `destroy = false` to retire a protected object safely, and use prevent_destroy sparingly because it makes some changes impossible to apply.

concepts.heading: ignore_changes and replace_triggered_by
concepts.body: `ignore_changes` lists attributes that Terraform ignores when planning updates after creation. It lets Terraform share an object with another process: if an autoscaler changes `desired_count`, `ignore_changes = [desired_count]` stops every plan from resetting it while other arguments stay managed. Only attributes defined by the resource type can be listed, not meta-arguments or lifecycle itself. The keyword `all` ignores every attribute, so Terraform can create and destroy the object but never plans updates. `replace_triggered_by` replaces a resource when a referenced resource, instance or attribute changes. The decision rests on planned actions of managed resources, so a local value or input variable cannot be listed. To rebuild a VM whenever `var.config_version` changes, store the variable in a `terraform_data` resource (`input = var.config_version`) and reference `terraform_data.version` in `replace_triggered_by`. A reference to a resource with several instances triggers if any instance is updated or replaced. Contrast the tools: `-replace` is a one-off on the command line, `replace_triggered_by` is a standing rule in code, and taint state comes from failed creation.

examPoints: A question that adopts many existing objects while a reviewer must see them first is testing import blocks (shown in plan, support for_each) over the terraform import command, which changes state immediately.
A question where deleting a resource block still destroys a protected database is testing that prevent_destroy lives in configuration, so removal needs a removed block with destroy = false.
A question about triggering a rebuild from a variable is testing that replace_triggered_by accepts only managed resources, so the value goes through a terraform_data resource.

quiz.q: A team applies an import block with `id = aws_instance.base.id`, but that instance is created in the same configuration during the same apply. What does terraform plan report?
choices: An error, because the id of an import block must be known during the plan operation
A plan that creates the instance first and then imports it in the same apply
A warning only, and the import is skipped until the next apply
A plan that replaces the instance so the id becomes known
quiz.explain: Import is planned before anything is created, so unknown ids are rejected. Choice B is tempting because Terraform orders dependencies, but import ids are needed at plan time. C and D describe behavior the docs do not support.

quiz.q: An engineer deletes a database's whole resource block, which had `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }`, and applies. What happens?
choices: Apply fails, because prevent_destroy is stored in state and still protects the database
Apply asks for the word destroy to be typed before continuing
Terraform destroys the database, because the rule was read from the configuration and left with the block
Terraform keeps the database and only removes it from state automatically
quiz.explain: Except for create_before_destroy, lifecycle rules are not kept in state, so removing the block removes the protection and plans a normal destroy. Use a removed block with destroy = false to stop managing it without deleting it.

days.recap: Import blocks show in plan, accept for_each (to = addr[each.key]), need ids known at plan time; the CLI command skips review. Move ownership by import first, then removed/state rm. create_before_destroy needs distinct names, prevent_destroy dies with its block, ignore_changes shares attributes, replace_triggered_by needs managed resources.

days.title: Multiple Environments and Troubleshooting Failed Runs

concepts.heading: Workspaces Versus One Root per Environment
concepts.body: A CLI workspace is a separate state instance inside the same working directory and backend; the docs describe it as technically equivalent to renaming the state file. Selecting a workspace changes only which state Terraform reads and writes, while the configuration, backend settings and credentials stay the same. That makes workspaces a poor isolation mechanism: auditors who find that dev credentials can run `terraform workspace select prod` and apply have found a design flaw, not a mistake. The docs name where workspaces fit: a parallel, throwaway copy of the infrastructure to test a change, often one workspace per feature branch, destroyed afterwards. For stages or teams that need separate credentials and access controls, the documented alternative is one small root module per environment (dev, stage, prod directories), each with its own backend and a few `module` blocks that instantiate shared modules. Costs are real: each directory has its own plugin and module cache, and updates from version control must be applied to each. Separate roots also let each environment pin its own module version, which is how a release is promoted from dev to prod.

concepts.heading: Keeping Environments Safe in Code
concepts.body: Two traps recur. First, nothing ties a variable file to a workspace. A pipeline that runs `terraform workspace select dev` and then `terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars` plans production sizes against dev state without any error. Guardrails: derive environment values from `terraform.workspace` in the root module (for example a map keyed by workspace name), use a directory per environment so the variable file and backend live together, or make the pipeline fail when the selected workspace and the variable file disagree. Second, `terraform.workspace` has the same value for every module call in a run. A shared module that names a bucket `"${terraform.workspace}-logs"` cannot be called twice, because the second call collides with the first and apply fails with a name that already exists. The references documentation warns such context values hurt module composability. The fix is an input such as `name_prefix`, with the root module computing each value (`"${terraform.workspace}-audit"`, `"${terraform.workspace}-access"`). Modules stay reusable, and only the root knows about environments.

concepts.heading: State Locks, Timeouts and Logs
concepts.body: Terraform locks state for every operation that can write it. A CI job killed in the middle of apply cannot release the lock, so the next run fails with Error acquiring the state lock and prints a lock ID and the holder's metadata. After confirming the earlier run is really dead, release it with `terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID`; the ID acts as a nonce so you unlock the right lock. Unlocking a lock another live run holds can create two writers, and `-lock=false` is not recommended because concurrent writers can corrupt state. When two healthy pipelines collide, the second fails at once because the default `-lock-timeout` is `0s`; add `-lock-timeout=10m` so it retries until the duration passes, ideally with a CI concurrency group that serializes runs. For diagnosis, `TF_LOG` turns on logging and sets the level (`TRACE` most verbose, then `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`) and writes to stderr. `TF_LOG_CORE` and `TF_LOG_PROVIDER` enable core and provider logs separately, so `TF_LOG_PROVIDER=DEBUG` investigates a failing API call without core noise. `TF_LOG_PATH` appends to a file but produces nothing unless `TF_LOG` is also set.

concepts.heading: Cycle Errors and Dependency Graph Problems
concepts.body: Terraform builds a dependency graph from references and `depends_on` and checks it for cycles before walking it. A plan that stops with Error: Cycle: aws_security_group.a, aws_security_group.b usually means two objects reference each other, the classic case being inline `ingress` blocks where each group uses the other's ID. Neither can be created first. `terraform graph -type=plan -draw-cycles` highlights the cycle edges (`-draw-cycles` works with an explicit `-type`). The fix is to break the loop by moving the part that creates the second edge into its own resource: define the rules as separate rule resources that depend on both groups, while the groups depend on nothing in each other. Adding `depends_on` cannot fix a cycle because it only adds edges. The same reasoning explains why you cannot set `create_before_destroy` to false on a dependency of a resource that has it. Remember the `-parallelism` setting, default 10 graph nodes at once on plan, apply and destroy, controls how many nodes run concurrently; the docs call it an advanced option and note providers such as AWS already back off and retry on rate limits.

concepts.heading: Validate Versus Plan and Missing Variables
concepts.body: Not every failure appears at the same stage. `terraform validate` checks syntax and internal consistency (attribute names, value types, references) regardless of variables or state, and it does not contact providers or remote services. It needs an initialized directory, and `terraform init -backend=false` prepares one without touching the backend. So a pipeline whose validate stage passes can still fail at plan with a provider authentication error, or with an instance size that has the right type but that no API accepts. Plan runs with a workspace, variable values and real credentials, includes an implied validation, and talks to the APIs while refreshing and reading data. Move such errors earlier with variable `validation` blocks or preconditions. Another common automation failure: `terraform plan -input=false` reports No value for required variable. A variable without a default needs a value from `-var`, `-var-file`, `terraform.tfvars`, `*.auto.tfvars`, a `TF_VAR_<name>` environment variable or HCP Terraform. A plain `prod.tfvars` is not loaded automatically, so either pass `-var-file=prod.tfvars` or export `TF_VAR_<name>`.

examPoints: A question where dev credentials can apply to prod is testing that CLI workspaces share one backend and credentials, so separate access needs a root module and backend per environment.

A question about a lock error after a cancelled job is testing that you confirm the holder is gone and run terraform force-unlock with the lock ID, while a lock collision between live runs calls for -lock-timeout.
A question where validate passes but plan fails is testing that validate never contacts providers or remote services.

quiz.q: A shared module names a bucket `"${terraform.workspace}-logs"`. A root module calls it twice as module.audit and module.access, and the second apply fails because the bucket name already exists. What is the correct fix?
choices: Run each module call in its own CLI workspace so the workspace names differ
Add depends_on from module.access to module.audit so they are created in order
Pass a name_prefix input from the root, using terraform.workspace only in the root module
Set create_before_destroy on the bucket so the names no longer collide
quiz.explain: terraform.workspace is identical for every module call in a run, so a name built from it alone collides. Choices A and B do not change the computed name, and D affects replacement order, not naming.

quiz.q: Two healthy pipelines apply to the same state. The second always fails immediately with a lock error although the first finishes within minutes. What makes the second wait?
choices: terraform force-unlock before each run
-lock=false on the second pipeline
TF_LOG_PATH set to a shared file
-lock-timeout=10m on plan and apply
quiz.explain: The default lock timeout is 0s, so Terraform fails at once; a duration makes it retry. Choice A could release a lock a live run holds, B risks corrupting state with two writers, and C only affects logging.

days.recap: Workspaces share backend and credentials; use a root and backend per environment for separation, and pass names into modules instead of terraform.workspace. Dead job: verify, force-unlock; live collision: -lock-timeout. TF_LOG needed for TF_LOG_PATH. Cycles: split resources. validate never calls APIs.

days.title: Passing Data Between Configurations and Managing Provider and Module Versions

concepts.heading: Reading Outputs in Scripts
concepts.body: Outputs leave a configuration in three ways: the human display, `terraform output`, and the state snapshot read by other configurations. In scripts, pick the format by data shape. The default display is HCL-like and shows sensitive values as `<sensitive>`. `-json` prints a JSON object with one key per output, or just the named output, and suits `jq`. `-raw` prints one value as a plain string with no formatting and supports only string, number and boolean, so `terraform output -raw subnet_ids` on a `list(string)` fails; use `terraform output -json subnet_ids` and parse it. Both `-json` and `-raw` print sensitive values in plain text, so treat the script log as sensitive. `-no-color` does not change the data shape, and `-state` is a legacy option for the local backend. Remember that marking an output `sensitive` only redacts display; the value remains in state, which is why anyone who can read a producer's state through `terraform_remote_state` can read far more than the one output they asked for. Outputs also need to be applied before they exist: adding an output in code does not put it into state until an apply.

concepts.heading: Remote State Versus tfe_outputs
concepts.body: Inside HCP Terraform you have two ways to read another workspace's outputs. `terraform_remote_state` reads the whole state snapshot and is governed by remote state sharing settings: new workspaces do not allow other workspaces to read their state by default, and the docs advise enabling access only between workspaces that need each other. The `tfe_outputs` data source from the tfe provider returns only output values, and the docs recommend it because it does not require full access to workspace state; remote state sharing controls do not apply to it. It still needs a tfe provider token with permission on the producing workspace, so an unshared workspace such as `vpc-prod` is readable through `tfe_outputs` only if that token may access it. When you are outside HCP Terraform, the documented alternatives avoid exposing state: a key/value or object store written with a resource and read with the matching data source (for example `consul_key_prefix` or `aws_s3_object`), or a DNS record with a predictable name resolved by a DNS data source. Choose by coupling: remote state is the tightest and needs no publishing step, the others add a step but narrow who can see what.

concepts.heading: Variable Precedence as a Diagnostic Tool
concepts.body: Predicting which value wins is a frequent Professional-level task. For root module variables the order, highest first, is: `-var` and `-var-file` on the command line (in the order given) together with variables set in HCP Terraform; `*.auto.tfvars` and `*.auto.tfvars.json` in lexical order; `terraform.tfvars.json`; `terraform.tfvars`; `TF_VAR_` environment variables; and the `default`. Conflicts are not errors; only assigning one variable twice in the same file is. Worked case: default `tiny`, `TF_VAR_size=xlarge`, `terraform.tfvars` small, `prod.auto.tfvars` large and `-var-file=ci.tfvars` medium gives medium. Lexical order is character order: `10-base.auto.tfvars` sorts before `2-team.auto.tfvars`, so the team file wins, and layered prefixes should be zero-padded. In HCP Terraform, workspace variables and variable sets rank above auto files and `terraform.tfvars`, so a workspace value of 5 beats `instance_count = 2` committed in `prod.auto.tfvars`. A value kept in two places means the reviewed file may not be what the run uses, so keep each variable in one place.

concepts.heading: Version Constraints Across Modules and the Lock File
concepts.body: A single provider version is installed for the whole configuration, and Terraform must satisfy the constraints of the root module and every child module together. If the root says `>= 5.0, < 5.10` and a registry module says `>= 5.20`, the intersection is empty and `terraform init` reports that no available release matches, listing which modules asked for what. Fix by raising the root bound after testing, choosing an older module version with a lower minimum, or relaxing one side. The recommendation for a shared module is a minimum only, `>=` the first release with the features it uses, because tighter pins in widely used modules block consumers; the root decides the final range. A pre-release such as `2.1.0-beta` is matched only by an exact version (`=` or no operator), never by `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` or `~>`. The lock file `.terraform.lock.hcl` records providers only. Remote modules are not remembered: a fresh CI workspace with `version = "~> 5.0"` takes the newest release in range, while a laptop that installed earlier keeps its copy, which explains plans that differ. Pin third-party modules to an exact version and move the pin in a reviewed change.

concepts.heading: Upgrading Deliberately and Changing Provider Source
concepts.body: `terraform init` reuses lock file selections and leaves installed modules alone, only installing what is new. `terraform init -upgrade` ignores lock selections, picks the newest provider matching the constraints, rewrites the lock file, and also updates installed child modules to the latest source matching their version constraints or refs. It never edits `.tf` files, changes the CLI version or migrates state. Review the lock file diff and the plan afterwards, in a lower environment first. To make CI fail when init would change the committed lock file, use `terraform init -lockfile=readonly`: it suppresses lock changes but still verifies installed packages against the recorded checksums, and it conflicts with `-upgrade`. Do not confuse it with `-backend=false` or `-get=false`. Each resource in state records its provider's fully qualified source address, so when a team moves from `hashicorp/aws` to an in-house `registry.acme.corp/acme/aws` and edits `required_providers`, plan fails because existing entries name the old address. Run `terraform state replace-provider registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws registry.acme.corp/acme/aws`, which writes a state backup first and asks for confirmation, then re-run init.

examPoints: A question where a script fails on terraform output -raw is testing that -raw handles only string, number and boolean, so lists and maps need -json with jq.
A question about reading another HCP Terraform workspace without full state access is testing tfe_outputs, which is not subject to remote state sharing but needs a token with permission.
A question where CI differs from a laptop after a new release is testing that the lock file covers providers only, so remote modules need an exact version pin.

quiz.q: A directory holds `10-base.auto.tfvars` (tier = "base") and `2-team.auto.tfvars` (tier = "team"). Nothing else sets tier. Which value does the root module use?
choices: base, because the file with the larger number loads first and the first value wins
team, because files load in lexical order and the later file wins
An error, because the same variable is set in two files
base, because numeric prefixes are compared as numbers
quiz.explain: Lexical order compares character by character, so 10-base sorts before 2-team and the later file wins. Choice C is wrong because duplicates are an error only inside one file; D is wrong because prefixes are not compared numerically.

quiz.q: The root module requires aws `>= 5.0, < 5.10` and a registry module requires `>= 5.20`. terraform init finds no available release. What is the cause?
choices: Terraform needs one version satisfying the root and all child module constraints together, and the ranges do not overlap
The lock file lists a different platform, so init cannot download the provider
Pre-release versions are blocked by the >= operator in the child module
Child modules may use their own provider version, and the registry rejected the second one
quiz.explain: All constraints are intersected because one provider version serves the whole configuration. Choice B concerns hashes, not ranges; C is unrelated to these numbers; D is wrong since a single version is shared.

days.recap: Output: -raw scalars only, -json for lists; tfe_outputs avoids full state access. Precedence: -var/-var-file and HCP vars > auto.tfvars (lexical) > terraform.tfvars > TF_VAR > default. Constraints intersect; modules want >= only; lock file is providers only; init -upgrade, -lockfile=readonly, state replace-provider.

days.title: CI/CD Pipeline Stages and Deployment Strategies with Terraform

concepts.heading: Pipeline Stages and Credential-Free Gates
concepts.body: A good pipeline is a sequence of gates, cheapest first, so most mistakes fail in seconds and without cloud access. Two gates need no credentials. `terraform fmt -check` reads only local files and exits 0 when formatting is canonical and non-zero, with file names, otherwise. By default `fmt` scans only the current directory, so a pipeline that must catch a badly formatted module under `modules/network/` uses `terraform fmt -check -recursive`. `terraform init -backend=false` followed by `terraform validate` catches syntax, attribute-name and type errors without touching the backend or any API. Validate does not test remote services, so an instance size that has the right type but that no provider API accepts passes validation and fails at plan; move such checks earlier with variable `validation` blocks or preconditions. Anything that reads real objects, a normal plan, a refresh-only plan and apply, needs the backend and provider credentials, so it belongs in a later stage on a runner that has them.

concepts.heading: Approval Gates and Saved Plan Artifacts
concepts.body: An approval gate is meaningful only if the thing reviewed is the thing that runs. If a pipeline plans on merge, a reviewer approves, and a later job runs `terraform apply -auto-approve` without a plan file, apply creates a new plan; anything that changed in between (another merge, a console edit, another pipeline) can appear unapproved, which is how a database got deleted that the reviewed plan never mentioned. The fix is to save the plan with `-out`, show it for review (`terraform show`), place the manual approval after it and apply that same file; if state moved meanwhile, Terraform refuses the stale plan. When plan and apply are separate jobs on different runners, remember: the artifact holds the full configuration and variable values and stores sensitive values in cleartext, so restrict access; the apply job must run `terraform init` with the same lock file and Terraform version because the plan file does not carry providers; and `-input=false` with no plan file and no `-auto-approve` fails, because with prompts disabled Terraform assumes you do not approve. Apply a saved plan or use `-auto-approve` deliberately, for example on an ephemeral environment.

concepts.heading: Exit Codes and HCP Terraform Runs
concepts.body: `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` returns 0 for success with no changes, 1 for an error and 2 for success with changes. A pipeline can then branch: 0 skips approval and apply, 2 raises the approval gate, 1 fails the build. A step that treats every non-zero code as failure will break on valid plans with pending changes, so capture the status and treat 2 explicitly. In HCP Terraform, a workspace connected to a repository starts a speculative plan when a pull request opens; it shows possible changes, is checked against policies, can never be applied and reruns when the pull request is updated. Pull requests from forks do not get one, to avoid running untrusted code or exposing sensitive information (on Terraform Enterprise an administrator can allow it), which explains a fork contribution with no plan while internal branches get one. Runs created through the API with the save-plan option are never auto-applied, even in a workspace with auto-apply enabled; they wait for confirmation, are discarded automatically if another run applies first, and ignore the per-workspace queue while planning. They suit custom CI that wants explicit approval of an exact plan.

concepts.heading: Blue/Green and Canary as Modeling Choices
concepts.body: Terraform has no deployment engine: it applies the state you declare, so a strategy is a way of modeling it. Blue/green keeps two complete stacks defined and uses one routing object, such as a load balancer listener, DNS weight or routing rule, to decide which receives traffic. A single variable such as `active_color` that changes only the listener's target makes cutover a tiny, reviewable plan, and rollback is the same one-line change because the old stack is still running. Remove the old stack later in a separate apply. A canary release (5 percent, 25, 100) needs configuration that feeds a weight variable (`canary_weight`) into a weighted target group or record, plus orchestration Terraform does not provide: the pipeline applies one step, evaluates metrics from a monitoring system, and runs the next apply only if the gate passes, or reapplies the previous value. Timers and provisioner sleeps are fragile and do not look at health. Each step should be a small plan; avoid `-target` for routine releases, because the docs reserve it for exceptional situations.

concepts.heading: Rolling Changes and Progressive Environments
concepts.body: A plan expresses the final state. If an AMI change forces replacement of twelve instances in one resource, the plan contains twelve replacements and the apply walks them as the graph allows; Terraform has no batch size. Plain Terraform can still roll in batches: put the instances in a `for_each` map keyed by group (`batch1`..`batch3`) with a per-group version value and move one group per apply, verifying between applies. Alternatively delegate rolling to a platform feature such as an autoscaling group's instance refresh and let Terraform change only the launch template. For promotion from dev to staging to prod, promote the same commit or module version tag through each environment and let environments differ only in variable values, each with its own backend and credentials. Per-environment branches or copied directories drift apart, and a floating branch reference makes what is deployed depend on the moment of the last init. In HCP Terraform, a run trigger queues a run in a workspace when a source workspace applies successfully, but runs created by a trigger do not auto-apply unless Auto-apply run triggers is enabled, which makes a handy promotion gate. Preview environments get their own state and are destroyed with it when the pull request closes.

examPoints: A question about an unformatted module that reached main is testing that terraform fmt -check covers only the current directory unless -recursive is added.
A question where the reviewed plan differs from what applied is testing that an approval gate must cover a saved plan file applied afterward, not a second fresh plan.
A question about canary or blue/green with Terraform is testing that cutover is a small variable-driven diff and that health checks and pacing come from pipeline orchestration, not from Terraform.

quiz.q: A pipeline step runs `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` and the build is marked failed on every run that has valid pending changes. What explains this?
choices: The flag makes plan return 1 whenever changes exist
Exit code 2 means success with changes, and the step treats any non-zero status as an error
The flag turns plan into an interactive prompt that times out
Exit code 0 is returned for changes, so the pipeline sees a missing apply
quiz.explain: With the flag: 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes present. The step must handle 2 explicitly. Choice A confuses the error code, C invents a prompt, and D reverses the meaning of 0.

quiz.q: A team promotes a change through dev, staging and prod and wants staging results to predict prod. Which practice fits best?
choices: Keep a branch per environment and cherry-pick fixes after each test
Point every environment at the main branch tip so they stay current
Copy the directory for each environment and edit the sizes by hand
Promote the same commit or module version tag, differing only in per-environment variable values
quiz.explain: Promotion works when the promoted unit is fixed and only inputs differ. Choices A and C drift apart, and B makes the deployed code depend on the moment of the last init.

days.recap: Cheap gates first: fmt -check -recursive, init -backend=false + validate (no API checks). Apply the exact saved plan after approval. -detailed-exitcode: 2 means changes. No speculative plans for forks; saved-plan runs never auto-apply. Blue/green = routing variable; canary needs pipeline metrics gates.

days.title: Dynamic Provider Credentials and Variable Files in Pipelines

concepts.heading: How Dynamic Credentials Work
concepts.body: Dynamic provider credentials replace long-lived cloud keys with a trust relationship. You configure the cloud platform to trust HCP Terraform as an OpenID Connect issuer and define rules for which workspaces and runs may assume which role. Then, for each plan and apply, HCP Terraform generates a workload identity token (OIDC) with claims about the organization, project, workspace and run stage, and sends it to the platform. The platform verifies the token with HCP Terraform's public signing key and, if its rules pass, returns fresh temporary credentials that HCP Terraform places in the run environment for the provider. Nothing static is stored in the workspace, so there is nothing to rotate or leak. On AWS the switch is the environment variable `TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH=true` together with a role ARN variable. The provider block must not fight this: the docs say to avoid the other arguments or methods in the provider's authentication documentation (such as static `access_key` and `secret_key` arguments or competing AWS environment variables) because they may interfere with dynamic credentials, which is why a workspace can still run as an old IAM user after dynamic credentials were enabled. Pass a region (the `region` argument or `AWS_REGION`).

concepts.heading: Writing the Trust Policy
concepts.body: The identity provider in AWS only trusts tokens from HCP Terraform's issuer; the role trust policy decides which tokens may assume the role. Tokens carry `aud`, the audience, which defaults to `aws.workload.identity` (or the value of `TFC_AWS_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_AUDIENCE`), and `sub`, shaped like `organization:ORG:project:PROJECT:workspace:WORKSPACE:run_phase:PHASE`. The default audience is public knowledge, so a condition on `aud` alone lets any workspace in any HCP Terraform organization that presents such a token assume the role. The docs say to check at minimum the audience and the organization name, and better the project and workspace through `sub`. Use `StringEquals` for one exact subject, or `StringLike` with `*` to cover a family of workspaces, scoped to the organization and project but no wider. Because `sub` ends in `run_phase:plan` or `run_phase:apply`, the run phase can be matched too. If plan and apply need different permissions, create two roles with two trust policies. If both phases can share one role, a single trust policy using `StringLike` with `*` after `run_phase:` accepts either.

concepts.heading: Per-Phase Roles, Sharing and Other Clouds
concepts.body: To make plans read-only and applies writable on AWS, create two roles whose trust policies match `run_phase:plan` and `run_phase:apply`, and set `TFC_AWS_PLAN_ROLE_ARN` and `TFC_AWS_APPLY_ROLE_ARN`. `TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN` is the fallback when a phase-specific variable is not set. To share one role across forty workspaces in a project, put `TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH=true` and `TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN` in a variable set applied to the project, and write a `sub` condition with `StringLike` wide enough for those workspaces; one change in the set then updates all of them. Azure uses federated identity credentials whose subject identifier must match the token subject exactly, as a direct string comparison, so each workspace needs two federated credentials, one for `run_phase:plan` and one for `run_phase:apply`; the audience defaults to `api://AzureADTokenExchange`. A symptom of the mistake is plans that authenticate while every apply fails. A workspace can also hold several configurations of one provider type by appending a tag to variable names (`[VAR_NAME]_[TAG]`); HCP Terraform then supplies a variable such as `tfc_aws_dynamic_credentials` with a default object and an aliases map, and each provider block, the default one included, must be mapped from it.

concepts.heading: Vault-Backed Credentials and Terraform Enterprise
concepts.body: Native dynamic credentials require the cloud platform to verify tokens itself. On Terraform Enterprise that means the cloud must reach the instance's OIDC metadata endpoints, `/.well-known/openid-configuration` and `/.well-known/jwks`. A company that will not expose those endpoints to the public internet can use Vault-backed dynamic credentials instead, which the HCP Terraform documentation describes: Vault trusts the workload identity token, and its AWS, GCP or Azure secrets engine generates the short-lived cloud credentials. Only Vault needs to reach the metadata endpoints, which do not have to be public, and the docs mention an air-gapped setup is possible when Vault is in the same secure network. Both approaches give each run short-lived credentials with no static secret in the workspace; the difference is who verifies the token and where the trust rules live. Vault-backed is the documented answer when network exposure of the Terraform instance is the constraint. In either case the permissions come from the role the token is allowed to assume, so least privilege is set in the cloud role and its trust policy.

concepts.heading: tfvars Files and Precedence in Pipelines
concepts.body: Without flags, Terraform loads only `terraform.tfvars`, `terraform.tfvars.json` and files ending in `.auto.tfvars` or `.auto.tfvars.json`. A file named `prod.tfvars` is ignored unless passed with `-var-file`, so per-environment files are either given the `.auto.tfvars` suffix (always on) or kept plain and selected explicitly in each pipeline step. Order of precedence, highest first: `-var` and `-var-file` on the command line and variables from HCP Terraform; `*.auto.tfvars` in lexical order; `terraform.tfvars.json`; `terraform.tfvars`; `TF_VAR_` environment variables; the `default`. With `terraform.tfvars` small, `prod.auto.tfvars` large and `TF_VAR_size=medium`, a plain `terraform plan` uses large. Numeric prefixes layer a base file under an override (`10-base`, `20-prod`) but are compared as text, so zero-pad them. Inside HCP Terraform, workspace variables and variable sets beat an auto.tfvars file in the uploaded directory. Variable sets have two layers: a priority variable set overrides variables with the same key at more specific scopes, with a prioritized global set at the top, while non-priority sets rank below workspace-specific variables, so a workspace variable overwrites them. Use priority sets for values that must not be overridden locally, such as a mandatory region.

examPoints: A question about a role trust policy checking only aud is testing that the default audience is public, so sub (organization, project, workspace, run phase) must be matched.
A question where plans authenticate but applies fail on Azure is testing that federated credential subjects match as exact strings, so both run_phase:plan and run_phase:apply credentials are needed.

A question about which tfvars file wins is testing the order: command line and HCP Terraform variables, auto.tfvars in lexical order, terraform.tfvars, TF_VAR, default, with priority variable sets above everything.

quiz.q: Dynamic AWS credentials are enabled in a workspace, yet runs still act as an old IAM user. The AWS provider block sets access_key and secret_key from variables. What should the team do?
choices: Raise the token lifetime so the temporary credentials outlast the static ones
Remove static credential arguments and conflicting AWS environment variables from the configuration
Add a second trust policy statement that allows the old IAM user to assume the role
Move the static keys into a non-priority variable set so they rank lower
quiz.explain: The docs say other authentication arguments and methods can interfere with dynamic credentials, so static keys and competing environment variables must go. Choice A and C do not change which credentials the provider uses, and D only changes variable precedence, not how the provider authenticates.

quiz.q: An organization-wide variable set marked as a priority set defines region = us-east-1 and applies to all workspaces. One workspace has its own variable region = eu-west-1. Which value do its runs use?
choices: eu-west-1, because workspace variables always override variable sets
The one declared in the repository's prod.auto.tfvars, because files in version control are authoritative
An error, because the same key is defined twice
us-east-1, because a priority global variable set overrides all other variables with the same key
quiz.explain: A prioritized global variable set sits at the top of the order. Only non-priority sets rank below workspace variables (choice A), auto files rank lower still (B), and conflicts are not errors (C).

days.recap: Dynamic credentials: OIDC token per plan/apply, trust policy must match sub, not just public aud. Separate plan/apply roles; Azure needs one federated credential per phase. Remove static keys. Vault-backed avoids exposing Enterprise endpoints. tfvars: only auto files load; priority variable sets win.
